Even if you have a card that earns cash back on your purchases, your rewards may post to your account in the form of points. The exact calculation of the cash back you can earn varies from card to card, but the accumulated rewards are typically added to your account once per statement cycle. When redeemed for cash back, each point likely has a monetary equivalent.

question: Will opening multiple credit cards help my credit score or hurt it if I’m worried about maxing them out?
answer: Having multiple credit cards can affect your credit score in both positive and negative ways, depending on how you manage them. Having more credit cards can increase your overall credit limit, which may lower your credit utilization ratio—the percentage of credit you're using compared to your total limit—and potentially boost your credit score. Note this may only happen if you don’t max out your cards and use all your credit. Maxing out your credit limit can lower your credit score. Applying for too many cards at once can also negatively impact your credit score, as each application results in a hard inquiry on your credit report.

question: Why does applying for a student credit card change if you're under 21?
answer: To apply for a student credit card, you may need to show proof of a steady income from a part-time or full-time job or have a co-signer (a person over the age of 21 with a steady income who takes responsibility for your late or missed payments) join you in the application process. The CARD Act of 2009 requires card issuers to assess independent income sources for applicants under the age of 21. People ages 18 to 21 applying for a credit card must show proof of independent income—unless they have a co-signer, usually a parent or guardian.

question: Why should I keep my credit card balance under $300 if my limit is $1,000?
answer: Keep your credit utilization ratio to 30% or lower: Your credit utilization ratio is the amount of credit you use compared to your total available credit. Using less than 30% of your total credit limit (e.g., keep spending under $300 on a $1,000 limit) shows loan providers you’re managing credit responsibly and could support a healthier credit score. It is generally a good idea to try to keep your credit utilization ratio below 30 percent. Keeping your ratio below 30 percent may positively impact your credit score.
